text: Isis and Ra’s Secret Name: When the Healer Is the One Who Caused the Harm
Ra had grown old.
Saliva fell from his mouth to the ground. Isis gathered this fluid from the god’s body, mixed it with earth, and made a snake.
She placed the snake on the road Ra traveled each day.
As Ra passed, the snake bit him.
Venom entered his body. Ra cried out in pain. The gods gathered, but none could undo this harm.
Isis came before him.
She knew spells, and knew how to make the venom leave.
But first she set a condition:
Tell me your secret name.
In this story, a name is no ordinary form of address.
Ra had many public names and could describe how he had created heaven and earth, brought forth rivers, and given life. He recited these one by one, but the venom did not stop.
Isis did not want more flattering facts about Ra.
She wanted the name intimately connected with his power, which he kept in his deepest recesses.
Only once the secret name had passed from Ra did Isis speak the words that drove the venom away.
She saved him.
She was also the very person who had made him need saving.
If Isis had merely happened by, found someone injured, and then sought compensation in exchange for healing, the story would already be complicated enough.
May a rescuer impose conditions in an emergency?
How far is an exchange someone agrees to in order to stay alive still a free choice?
But this story goes further.
Isis did not exploit a danger that had arisen by chance.
She created the danger.
The snake came from her knowledge, its placement on his route was her doing, and the wound was part of the plan. Then she appeared as the only person able to undo the harm.
This means that “healing” cannot wash away what came before.
She really did heal Ra.
But she cannot therefore be understood solely as a healer.
If someone first pushes another into a predicament only they can solve, then says “I am willing to help, provided you surrender what I want,” the help is only the second half of the action.
The first half still determines what the second half means.
In life, “I can solve your problem” often brings power.
That power is not necessarily wrong in itself.
Someone who genuinely possesses knowledge, resources, or ability may indeed propose terms of exchange. They need not abandon every boundary merely because others need them.
But when the person offering help has helped create the need, the condition is no longer merely compensation.
It is closer to a choice with the exits closed:
Give up the secret, or go on suffering.
When Ra finally speaks his name, formally it remains an act he performs with his own mouth.
But looking only at “Did he say yes?” leaves out the setting in which the choice occurred.
When the only alternative to one answer is continuing harm, consent has not vanished altogether, but it has been compressed.
This does not mean that every decision made in a crisis is invalid.
People can still choose in danger, and may sincerely consider the exchange worthwhile.
The point is that the person who created the danger cannot use the other’s eventual agreement to prove that the process of imposing the condition was therefore legitimate.
Consent can tell us what the trapped person chose from the possibilities left to them.
It cannot relieve the person who set the trap of responsibility for creating the situation.
What Isis wanted was the name.
Why would a name bring such great power?
In this ancient Egyptian narrative, a name is not a label attached to the outside of a being. Possessing the true name means being able to act upon the other at a deeper level.
Ra first gives many public identities: what he has done, what he is called, and what powers he governs.
All of these are true.
But Isis knows that describing someone’s attributes is not the same as obtaining the key to their deepest self.
She is not satisfied with understanding Ra.
She wants to change who can act upon whom in their relationship.
This makes the boundary between “knowing someone” and “having power over someone” clear.
We often treat transparency as closeness, and knowing more as making a relationship more authentic.
But some information is protected for reasons beyond a fear of being misunderstood.
It changes how others can affect us.
Secrecy may provide cover for evading responsibility.
It may also be a condition for retaining room to decide for oneself.
So the mere existence of a piece of knowledge does not give the closest, cleverest, or most capable person a natural right to obtain it.
That Ra’s public names do not satisfy Isis does not prove that he has deceived her.
It may instead mean he knows that, once certain knowledge is handed over, the relationship can never return to its previous shape.
Yet if we only criticize Isis, the story becomes too smooth.
Ra is no ordinary victim.
He stands high in the divine order, holding secrets and powers Isis cannot obtain through an ordinary request.
Why must Isis use a snake, venom, and a scheme?
The text offers no open, equal path by which she could present reasons and gain the same standing.
Those in a weaker position confronting closed power often have only indirect means available.
If we say only “She should have asked honestly,” we may be pretending that an honest request would actually be heard within that order.
This creates a genuine difficulty for judgment.
Can an unjust power structure make deception one of the few available methods?
If so, must the person using deception still answer for the harm they cause?
We cannot simply choose an easy answer.
Weakness does not automatically justify every means.
Otherwise, Ra’s suffering would lose its weight merely because he possesses power.
But requiring the weak to use only methods already approved by the strong may also make existing disparities impossible to change.
The story’s sharpness lies precisely in making Isis neither simply a villain nor simply a liberator.
Her route to power exposes the lack of a normal route within the existing order.
At the same time, it makes another being’s body into a tool.
Isis’s knowledge runs through the entire action.
She knows what power Ra’s saliva carries.
She knows how to make the snake, how to make the gods unable to heal, and the final spell.
Knowledge here both causes harm and removes it.
That makes “knowledge itself is good” seem too simple.
The same ability can open a path to healing or create a wound that only its possessor can heal.
What truly requires judgment is not only how much someone knows, but what relationships they bring that knowledge into.
Some abilities earn trust because they solve problems.
That trust may in turn lead people to overlook whether the capable person is constantly creating new dependencies.
A consultant can explain matters in a way that leaves only them able to keep explaining.
An organization can first remove its members’ choices, then call restoring a few of them “care.”
Someone who controls a crucial resource can make those around them ever more dependent, then treat that dependence as proof that they are irreplaceable.
This does not mean that all professional help manufactures dependence.
It only reminds us:
The ability to solve problems does not exempt the solver from explaining why problems always arise in ways that require them.
Ra finally surrendered his secret name, and Isis did indeed keep her promise.
She did not leave him to die after obtaining the name.
This still distinguishes her from a mere extortionist.
Her offer of exchange was not pure falsehood.
She really gave the healing that only she could provide.
But fulfilling a transaction does not change how the transaction was established.
Someone can honestly carry out the second half they promised in an unjust situation, while the first half still requires judgment.
That is also why “The outcome was good” cannot settle the whole action’s account on its own.
Isis gained power, Ra gained life, and the spell in the story was later used by others against snake venom.
These real benefits do not undo the fact that the snake was created.
Conversely, the creation of the snake does not make the healing false.
It is easy to wish an action had only one name: rescue or harm; resistance or control; wisdom or deception.
This story refuses that neatness.
Isis is at once the one who harms, a healer, a seeker of knowledge, and a challenger of power.
Any account that keeps only one side removes the story’s most important difficulty.
This narrative originally also belonged to the context of spells for treating venom.

It does not only recount a sacred event in the past; it also provides language and efficacy for actual healing rituals. Isis finally commands the venom to leave Ra, and the reciter uses that same story to address the poisoning before them.
We therefore cannot treat it entirely as a modern ethical short story.
Names, spells, bodies, and sacred precedents are linked within it, in ways far more complex than “someone has the password.”
But precisely because the healing context is there, the story’s paradox is harder to overlook:
The authority to heal comes from a wound designed by the healer herself.
Healing knowledge thus deserves reliance, yet must also be examined.
Truly reliable care depends not only on whether suffering can be stopped in the end.
It also depends on whether that care needs others to become powerless first in order to prove its own power.
Isis ultimately obtained Ra’s secret name.
Not because Ra calmly decided to trust her.
Nor because the two rearranged power through shared reasons.
The name was surrendered while venom still remained in his body.
The victory in the story therefore always carries a wound.
We can understand why someone uses a scheme within a closed order.
We can acknowledge her intelligence, patience, and keeping of her word.
We can also see why the existing power made an ordinary request almost impossible.
But understanding this does not require us to rename harm as part of healing.
A helper does not acquire the exclusive right to interpret an earlier injury simply by later saving the person injured.
Nor can someone weaker, because their goal is to break down a disparity, reduce the injured person to a mere symbol of oppressive power.
Isis made the venom leave Ra.
She did not make the path by which she obtained his name harmless.
Perhaps the question this story truly leaves behind is not who ended up stronger.
It is why a world closes off power to such an extent
that anyone seeking to approach it must first create a wound only they can heal.

*Textual basis: the ancient Egyptian tradition of the snakebite-healing spell “Isis and Ra’s Secret Name,” preserved in various papyri and ostraca from the New Kingdom. This essay follows the continuous account in which Isis makes a snake from Ra’s saliva and earth, poisons him, and demands his secret name as a condition of healing; Ra first lists public names and creative accomplishments, but the venom persists; after the secret name is transferred, Isis commands the venom to depart. It retains the narrative’s ritual function as a healing spell, does not simply equate the “secret name” with a modern password, and does not reduce Isis to a pure heroine or a pure villain.*
